summary: How an architect decides, records the reason, and runs a kata or a 45-minute interview.

blocks.title: A kata in five steps
rows: Find the two or three hard sentences. Set the scope.
Select the few that drive the design. Tie each to a kata sentence.
Select the simplest style that supports the characteristics.
One job for each box. Show data owners. Label each arrow.
Write what the design is bad at, and where it fails first.

blocks.title: When you see this, do this

items.when: A decision is expensive to change later
items.use: It is architecture. The architect decides.

items.when: A decision is about one class or one module pattern
items.use: Let the team that writes the code decide
The one that is easier to change later

items.when: A decision is cheap to delay and you will know more later
items.use: Delay it. Say what you wait for.

items.when: A decision is hard to reverse, or the team argued about it
The interviewer has no answer to your question
You select the part for the deep dive
items.use: The hardest part. Say why it is hardest.

items.text: If you cannot name the cost of your choice, your analysis is not finished.
State the decision as a question. A vague question gives a vague answer.
List two or three real options. Include the simplest one, even if you expect to reject it.
Score each option as better, worse, or the same. Write one sentence of reason for each score.
Write: "We select A because of X. We accept Y. We will look again if Z occurs."
A design with no stated cost is a sales text.
"Large companies use microservices" is not a reason. Their constraints are not yours.
Team size, budget, deadline, and the law decide more than the technology does.
An ADR holds one decision and its reason. Keep ADRs with the code, with a number for each.
An ADR has five parts: title, status, context, decision, and consequences.
One page is the usual limit. A longer ADR probably holds more than one decision.
Write the consequences that hurt. A future reader needs them.
Never edit an accepted ADR to change the decision. Write a new ADR that replaces it.
The rationale box in a kata is a small ADR: forces, decision, and consequences.

items.label: Length of a system design interview
Ask questions and set the scope
Go deep on one or two hard parts
Driving characteristics to select
items.note: The app lets you select up to five.

items.text: Do not start to draw immediately. Ask what you need for the design first.
Think aloud. A correct diagram drawn in silence usually does worse.
Do not design for a scale that the problem did not ask for.
Say what job each part does. A product name like Kafka is not enough.
Put a name on each box and a label on each arrow: does the caller wait?
Do not defend the design when the interviewer shows a problem. A hint is a gift.
Finish with what fails first, why you accepted it, and what you would look at next.
Answer a behavioral question with one true story: situation, task, action, result, and what you learned.
Keep 8 to 12 stories ready. Say "I" for your actions, and give a number in the result.
End each story with one sentence about what you learned or would change. It shows judgment.
